system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2198-11-28 02:45:00 to 2198-12-01 11:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of Type 1 diabetes and gastroparesis was admitted for severe nausea and vomiting, consistent with a gastroparesis flare. She had elevated blood glucose levels and required IV fluids and medication adjustments. A chest X-ray revealed a small left lower lobe pneumonia, likely due to aspiration from vomiting, and she was treated with levofloxacin and metronidazole. An EGD with Botox injection was performed, after which her symptoms improved and she advanced to a soft diet. Her blood pressure, initially elevated, normalized with treatment. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete her antibiotic course, continue adjusted insulin therapy, and follow up with gastroenterology and endocrinology. Iron deficiency anemia was noted and recommended for outpatient monitoring.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU because your blood sugar was very high and you’re in diabetic ketoacidosis. We’ve started you on fluids and insulin through an IV to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’ve been here before for this. I took my Lantus this morning and used my sliding scale, but I just couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 637 when you arrived, and your anion gap was elevated, which confirms DKA. We’re giving you an insulin drip now to bring that down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous all day. Started vomiting around 7 p.m. I didn’t eat much. Is that why this happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a big part of it. Poor intake and vomiting can throw off your insulin balance. We’re also treating your nausea with Zofran and Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still feeling shaky and my heart’s racing. Is that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the high blood sugar and dehydration can cause tachycardia—your heart rate is 129. We’re watching it closely. It should improve as we correct your fluids and sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw some peaked T-waves on your EKG, and your potassium was high at 5.6. We’re monitoring that carefully to prevent any heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s scary. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We caught it early. Your levels are coming down with treatment. No signs of a heart attack—we checked your enzymes and they were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had so many DKA episodes because of my gastroparesis. The Botox didn’t help much last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you had an EGD with Botox recently. Unfortunately, it sounds like it hasn’t provided lasting relief. We’re focusing on symptom control for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed some dark flecks in my vomit. Is that blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Given your history of esophagitis, it could be from irritation in your esophagus. We’ve started you on an IV proton pump inhibitor to protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable. The dark flecks are likely old blood. We’ll keep an eye on it, but you’re not showing signs of active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from a few hours ago show your glucose is down to 217 and your anion gap is closing. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little less shaky. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We want to make sure your nausea is under control and your sugars stay stable. We’ll try small sips later if you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been off my blood pressure meds—metoprolol and lisinopril. Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held them initially because your blood pressure and heart rate were high from DKA. Once you’re more stable, we’ll restart them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your urine test back. There was a possible E. coli, so we started you on cipro just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have any burning when I pee. Could it be a false alarm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The lab noted contamination from skin flora, so it might not be a real infection. We’ll repeat the test and stop antibiotics if it’s negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat urine culture showed contamination again. No true UTI. We’re stopping the cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I didn’t want to take more antibiotics. I’m still on metronidazole—should I stop that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were supposed to finish that course a few days ago. Since you’re still taking it, we’ll have you stop now to avoid unnecessary side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your anion gap is now normal, and your blood sugars are between 150 and 200. We’re switching you from the insulin drip to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go back to my Lantus and Humalog?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll get 30 units of Lantus at bedtime and use Humalog as a sliding scale four times a day. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I was on before. I hope it keeps me stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today. No signs of pneumonia. Your lungs look clear, which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had pneumonia last time I was here. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lungs are clear. The previous opacity has resolved. This time, your DKA was triggered by gastroparesis, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated a small meal earlier without vomiting. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I actually felt hungry. Can I eat more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance your diet slowly—soft foods first. Your nausea has improved, so that’s promising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I hate being on IV fluids. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep doing well—eating, stable sugars, no vomiting—we’re looking at discharge tomorrow or the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are excellent. Anion gap closed, no ketones, sugars 100–180. You’ve had two meals without issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your metoprolol and lisinopril. Your blood pressure is now well-controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Nexium? I wasn’t taking it, but I know I should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to pantoprazole 40 mg daily. It’s similar and will help with your esophagitis and those dark flecks in your vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor your blood sugar closely. If you start vomiting again or can’t keep food down, check for ketones and come in early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Should I follow up with my endocrinologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within a week. Also with GI to discuss long-term options for your gastroparesis. The Botox hasn’t helped much, so other treatments may be needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. All set for discharge. You’re on Lantus 30 units at bedtime, Humalog sliding scale, and your other meds as we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No changes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Continue everything as prescribed. Take the pantoprazole daily, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me get through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and don’t hesitate to call or come in if things go off track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to prevent that. Take care, and I’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of Type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis, and esophagitis was admitted for diabetic ketoacidosis triggered by poor oral intake and vomiting. She was treated in the ICU with an insulin drip, which was transitioned to subcutaneous insulin as her anion gap closed and blood sugars stabilized. Nausea and vomiting improved with antiemetics, and she advanced to a soft diet. A possible UTI was ruled out due to urine contamination, and antibiotics were discontinued. Her home antihypertensives were restarted, and she was switched to pantoprazole for esophagitis. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to continue her insulin regimen, take pantoprazole daily, and follow up with endocrinology and gastroenterology.
